records.title: gpytorch-gp-predict: accuracy_supported=False; continuous_lg timeouts at n≥500; nongauss timing anomaly; discrete/hybrid unimplemented
records.body:
**Note (v0.13 cutover, PR #119):** The original adapter at `benchmarking/baselines/gpytorch_adapter.py` was deleted along with the entire `benchmarking/baselines/` package. v0.8 work would implement a new `BaselineAdapter` subclass in `benchmarking/adapters/gpytorch_adapter.py` using the v0.13 stateful protocol.

---

## Summary

gpytorch-gp-predict is currently the only third-party continuous-domain
baseline in our benchmark. Four gaps prevent it from being a usable
comparison point:

1. **`accuracy_supported=False` in registry** — no distributional accuracy
   metric (W1/JSD/TV) is produced for *any* cell. Only `total_time_s` is
   recorded. This is an explicit registry policy, but the rationale is
   undocumented and the paper consequence is severe.
2. **continuous_lg timeouts at n≥500** — 4/5 seeds timeout at n=500,
   all 5 at n=1000. Expected for exact GP (O(n³)), but needs investigation
   and documentation.
3. **continuous_nongauss timing anomaly** — completes in ~0.9–1.3s at
   *all* sizes including n=1000, while continuous_lg times out at n=500.
   This asymmetry is suspicious and warrants investigation (is the GP
   actually running, or falling through silently?).
4. **Discrete and hybrid: not_supported** — intentional registry gate,
   but undocumented and unresolved as a deliberate scope decision.

Without distributional accuracy numbers, the paper has no third-party
baseline to compare against on continuous_nongauss. The contribution
claim "NBN is competitive with gpytorch" cannot be supported.

## Empirical evidence (merged parquet, master post-PR-#93)

### Registry entry

```python
"gpytorch-gp-predict": BaselineApplicability(
    frozenset({"continuous_lg", "continuous_nongauss"}),
    accuracy_supported=False,
),
```

### Status breakdown

```
status                              not_supported  ok  timeout
family              n_nodes metric
continuous_lg       10      accuracy            5   0        0
                            total_time_s        0   5        0
                    50      accuracy            5   0        0
                            total_time_s        0   5        0
                    100     accuracy            5   0        0
                            total_time_s        0   5        0
                    500     accuracy            1   0        0   ← 4 timed out before accuracy
                            status              0   0        4   ← timeout
                            total_time_s        0   1        0   ← only 1 completed
                    1000    status              0   0        5   ← all timeout
continuous_nongauss 10-1000 accuracy            5   0        0   ← not_supported at all sizes
                            total_time_s        0   5        0   ← ok at all sizes
discrete            all     status              5   0        0   ← not_supported (intentional)
hybrid              all     status              5   0        0   ← not_supported (intentional)
```

### Timing for completed cells (total_time_s, ok rows only)

| family | n_nodes | seeds | time range (s) |
|--------|---------|-------|----------------|
| continuous_lg | 10 | 5 | 0.004–1.13 |
| continuous_lg | 50 | 5 | 1.03–1.53 |
| continuous_lg | 100 | 5 | 1.01–1.61 |
| continuous_lg | 500 | 1 | 2.39 (4/5 timeout) |
| continuous_lg | 1000 | 0 | all timeout |
| continuous_nongauss | 10–1000 | 5 | 0.88–1.26 |

The nongauss times at n=1000 (~1.0s) are indistinguishable from n=10
(~0.9s), which is not consistent with any GP inference. For comparison,
continuous_lg at n=500 already takes 2.4s (1 seed) before timing out.

## Investigation requested

### Q1: Why is `accuracy_supported=False`?

Options:
- **(a) Output type mismatch**: gpytorch returns a Gaussian posterior
  (`MultivariateNormal`), not samples. The W1/accuracy computation
  requires samples or a CDF. Fix: draw samples from the posterior
  distribution before passing to the metric.
- **(b) Deliberate exclusion**: GP predict was added as a timing-only
  baseline (wall-clock comparison). If so: document this in the registry
  and in the paper. "Timing-only" is a weaker comparison point — note
  it explicitly.
- **(c) Placeholder**: `accuracy_supported=False` was set during
  development and never revisited.

Verify by reading `benchmarking/baselines/gpytorch_adapter.py` and the
metric pipeline. If the fix is drawing samples from the posterior, it
is likely a 2–5 line change.

### Q2: continuous_nongauss timing anomaly

The ~1s constant timing across all nongauss sizes (n=10 to n=1000) is
not consistent with GP inference:
- Exact GP: O(n³) training, O(n²) prediction
- At n=1000 we'd expect ~1000× the time of n=10, not the same

Hypotheses:
- **(a) Silent fallback**: the adapter catches an exception on nongauss
  input (e.g. data type / shape mismatch) and returns a dummy result
  in ~1s without actually running the GP.
- **(b) Cached model**: the GP is trained on a subset or reused across
  cells (bug in adapter state isolation).
- **(c) GPU fast path**: GPU inference makes it genuinely fast (but then
  why does continuous_lg still time out?).

Check the adapter's exception handling and whether it validates that
inference actually ran.

### Q3: continuous_lg timeout at n≥500

Exact GP inference is O(n³) — timeouts at n=500/1000 are expected.
Decision needed:
- Accept the coverage gap and document it (gpytorch is timing-only,
  and only at n≤100 reliably).
- Switch to sparse/approximate GP (e.g. `gpytorch.models.ApproximateGP`
  with inducing points) for large n.
- Raise `per_cell_timeout_s` only for gpytorch at large n (runner
  supports per-baseline timeouts?).

### Q4: Discrete / hybrid extension

GP classification (Laplace/EP/variational) is standard in gpytorch:
- `gpytorch.likelihoods.BernoulliLikelihood` for binary
- `gpytorch.likelihoods.SoftmaxLikelihood` + `VariationalGP` for
  multiclass (matches our discrete cardinality=4 setting)

Decision needed: add to registry and implement adapter, or document
as exp

records.title: fix(core): cascade agent.kill to child agents, grants, and agent homes
records.body:
## Problem

`kill_agent` removes one agent, cancels only that agent's sessions and workers, and deletes only that agent's metadata file. It does not walk `parent_agent_id`, revoke workspace grants, or remove the on-disk agent home created at spawn.

`spawn_agent_record` still enforces parent existence, `child_count`, and `agent_depth`. After a mid-tree kill, descendants stay live with a dangling parent. `agent_depth` stops when the parent record is missing, so a former depth-2 agent is measured as depth 1 and can spawn another generation under the default `max_depth = 2`. Tests only cover killing a leaf and rejecting `main`.

**Evidence:**
- `crates/cadis-core/src/lib.rs:2362-2419` — `kill_agent` has no child walk, grant revoke, or home cleanup
- `crates/cadis-core/src/lib.rs:2302-2332` — spawn still enforces `max_total_agents`, `max_children_per_parent`, and `max_depth`
- `crates/cadis-core/src/lib.rs:5705-5716` — `agent_depth` walks live parent links and stops when the parent is gone
- `crates/cadis-core/src/lib.rs:2358` — `profile_home.init_agent` on spawn; never reversed on kill
- `crates/cadis-core/src/lib.rs:2532-2575` and `crates/cadis-core/src/workspace.rs:247-252` — grants persist independently of agent lifetime
- `crates/cadis-core/src/lib.rs:14184-14237` — tests cover leaf kill and `cannot_kill_main_agent` only

Neighboring issues (do not duplicate): #403 guards `agent_depth` against cycles in recovered parent chains; #895 is UI-configurable spawn caps. This issue is kill-time cleanup and the resulting depth-limit bypass.

## Actual Output

```text
spawn A under main (depth 1)
spawn B under A (depth 2; max_depth=2)
agent.kill A
-> A removed; B still in Runtime.agents with parent_agent_id=A
-> B sessions/workers/grants/home still live
-> agent_depth(B) == 1 because A is gone
-> spawn C under B is accepted (measured depth 2) even though the original chain is main→A→B→C
```

## How to Fix

1. In `kill_agent`, collect descendants whose `parent_agent_id` chain includes the killed agent (BFS/DFS) and kill them in child-first order, or explicitly reparent and document that policy.
2. Revoke workspace grants whose `agent_id` matches each killed agent; persist via `persist_workspace_grants`.
3. Remove or archive the profile agent home created by `init_agent`.
4. Keep emitting `agent.killed` for every agent actually removed so HUD/CLI can drop roster rows.
5. Add a unit test: spawn A then B, kill A, assert B is gone (or reparented), grants for A/B are gone, and a further spawn still respects the original `max_depth`.

## Expected Output

```text
agent.kill A
-> A and descendants cancelled; their sessions, workers, grants, and homes cleaned up
-> agent.killed events for each removed agent
-> spawn depth still measured against the original tree policy
```

## Critical Level

**Medium** — local protocol, but it bypasses spawn-depth policy and leaves tool-capable orphans plus grants.

## My Confidence

**High** — kill path, depth walk, and tests verified at HEAD `52c5585`; no descendant walk exists.

## Why Matters?

Spawn limits are a documented resource control. Killing a mid-level specialist should not leave children running tools or make `max_depth` cheaper to evade. CLI/HUD kill UX (companion issues) is unsafe until this cascade exists.

records.title: Map: blast-radius diagnosis and graph-based codebase navigation
records.body:
## Destination

Two decisions, resolved independently on this one map:

- **Thread A — Blast-radius diagnosis**: Is "blast radius" (context/navigation cost) actually why implementation sessions in this fork's workflow creep into the dumb zone? Resolved via lightweight evidence (mining the user's own past session transcripts/tickets, not formal benchmarking — no repeatable-experiment budget or benchmarking background available) plus theoretical reasoning. Output is either a confirmed cause (and shape of mitigation) or a redirect to the real cause.
- **Thread B — Graph-tooling adoption**: Should this fork adopt a graph-encoded codebase-navigation tool (candidates so far: Graphify-Labs/graphify, GitNexus, code-review-graph) for `to-spec`/`to-tickets`/`implement`, and if so, source-code-only or wider scope (issues/specs/ADRs too)? Resolved via structured research (what's encoded, staleness handling, integration cost, provenance/trust) before any hands-on trial — not naive parallel trial of 3+ tools.

## Notes

- Scope: local fork (`HarrisRamosBaroni/skills`) experimentation only. No intent to upstream to `mattpocock/skills` (upstream isn't accepting new collaborators / PRs from non-collaborators anyway).
- Source-only-vs-wider graph scope is genuinely open — do not pre-decide it; Thread B's research settles it.
- Caution: initial research found anomalous star-to-age ratios on all three graph-tool candidates (e.g. Graphify-Labs/graphify: ~109K stars at ~4.5 months old with ~30 real contributors, and an install command pointing at a differently-spelled package `graphifyy`, a pattern consistent with typosquatting). Treat GitHub star counts as unreliable signal; verify provenance/trustworthiness before evaluating substance.
- Default to `/grilling` and `/domain-modeling` for HITL tickets on this map.
- Related upstream context (not binding): https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/issues/887 proposes an optional Graphify-aware navigation protocol for `to-spec`/`to-tickets`/`implement`. Useful shape reference for Thread B, not a settled answer.

## Decisions so far

## Not yet specified

- If Thread A confirms blast radius is the cause **and** Thread B lands on adopting a graph tool: how exactly the tool gets wired into `to-spec`/`to-tickets`/`implement` (mirrors the shape in upstream issue #887) — can't specify until both threads resolve.
- If Thread A finds a different cause than blast radius: what the alternative fix path looks like — can't specify without knowing the alternative cause.

## Out of scope

records.title: WORKFLOW-FINAL-REVIEW-EVIDENCE-READBACK-01 — exact candidate evidence for ChatGPT final review
records.body:
## Status

`APPROVED — ACTIVE IMPLEMENTATION NODE / LOCAL-ONLY CANDIDATE`

This node is activated by explicit user approval on 2026-08-24. It is the current P0-1 item from #285.

## Goal

Close the current ChatGPT-first lifecycle gap after `run-reviewbundle`:

`Codex candidate -> deterministic candidate identity -> exact candidate readback -> ChatGPT actual-content review -> ACCEPTED / focused repair`

The user must not be required to upload candidate files, paste diffs, interpret SHA/fingerprints, or act as a technical evidence relay.

## Current blocker / dogfood target

Issue #284 already has an unstaged/uncommitted two-file candidate and trusted review bundle comment `5394902606`.

That bundle proves scope/fingerprint/manifest and `git diff --check`, but ChatGPT cannot independently retrieve the actual local candidate content. A same-node reviewer-evidence probe then failed closed with `same_node_continuation_launcher_binding_missing`.

The implementation must preserve #284 unchanged and later use it as the first real readback dogfood target.

## Required outcome

Implement the smallest deterministic readback path inside the existing B3 / Dispatcher / Runner architecture. Prefer activating the already-reserved `read-final-audit` action rather than inventing a parallel transport unless repository contracts make that incorrect.

A readback request must bind to trusted existing candidate evidence, including at least:

- repository
- target Issue
- trusted parent review-bundle comment identity
- branch / base HEAD
- allowed candidate files
- candidate manifest/fingerprint (or stronger equivalent)

Before any evidence leaves the local host, deterministic code must re-read and verify the local candidate against that binding.

## Evidence transport requirements

ChatGPT must be able to retrieve the exact candidate unified diff and/or exact text snapshots from the existing GitHub result surface without asking the user to relay local files.

Remote evidence publication is permitted only for this exact bounded reviewer-readback action and must:

1. be request-bound and candidate-bound;
2. publish only files allowed by the original candidate Task Packet / manifest;
3. reject extra or changed files, wrong branch/HEAD, tampered candidate, untrusted/mismatched parent evidence, or stale/ambiguous identity;
4. reject binary/unsupported content rather than silently converting it;
5. run deterministic sensitive-content checks and fail closed on credential/secret-like material rather than redact an allegedly exact snapshot;
6. enforce explicit payload/chunk limits with complete sequence + digest verification; no silent truncation;
7. use a dedicated machine-readable evidence marker/protocol and exact chunk/order/digest metadata if chunking is needed;
8. never treat successful evidence publication as final acceptance.

## Dirty-candidate semantics

A valid reviewed candidate is expected to be dirty. The readback path must distinguish an exact reviewer-ready dirty candidate from arbitrary dirty worktree state. It must never permit dirty-state execution merely because a request says `expected_state`; local state must match trusted candidate evidence exactly.

## Authority / hard boundaries

Allowed:

- bounded modifications to existing Bridge / Dispatcher / Runner implementation and directly related tests;
- minimal update to an existing canonical runbook/spec only if required to keep the implemented action contract truthful;
- targeted + adjacent tests;
- one focused repair;
- exact remote Issue-comment publication only for deterministic reviewer evidence under the new bounded action;
- live dogfood against the preserved #284 candidate after implementation evidence is reviewed.

Forbidden:

- modification, restore, reset, staging, commit, or publication of the #284 candidate;
- automatic final acceptance;
- automatic commit/push/PR/merge/Issue close/label mutation;
- generic GitHub contents writes or branch ref mutation;
- credentials/authentication/PATH/dependency/package changes;
- service, daemon, new scheduler, tray, MCP, Desktop Agent, UI, or second runtime owner;
- broad filesystem reads or broad Issue scanning;
- scope expansion beyond reviewer evidence readback.

## Acceptance

1. A trusted existing review bundle can authorize only one exact reviewer-evidence readback for its exact candidate state.
2. ChatGPT can retrieve actual candidate content, not only summary/hash metadata.
3. Candidate tampering, extra files, wrong branch/HEAD, wrong Issue/parent, wrong manifest, unsupported/binary data, unsafe content, oversize/incomplete chunks all fail closed before a false complete-evidence claim.
4. Readback does not invoke Codex as part of evidence retrieval and does not stage/commit/push/PR/merge/close or mutate candidate files.
5. Tests cover success plus identity mismatch, candidate tamper, extra file, sensitive-content rejection, unsupported/binary rejection, payload/chunk completeness, and remote-write failure/uncertainty semantics.
6. Existing `maybe-status-check` and `run-reviewbundle` paths remain compatible.
7. #284 live dogfood produces complete exact evidence retrievable by ChatGPT, after which ChatGPT can issue the #284 actual-content verdict without user file relay.
8. Runtime is returned to a healthy bounded state after dogfood.

## Current baseline

- repository: `HarryWhite-TW/local-ai-workbench`
- canonical remote baseline: `master@590c4c4789ac784d81147c079fddc9bcef15a7c3`
- implementation branch target: `codex/workflow-final-review-evidence-readback-01`
- #284 candidate remains in the existing engineering worktree and must be preserved.

## Task Packet

LOCAL-RUNNER-TASK-PACKET-V1
BEGIN_TASK_PACKET
protocol: lawb.local_runner.task_packet.v1.1
packet_id: workflow-final-review-evidence-readback-01-r1
logical_issue: 286
phase: comfortable_daily_loop_closure_integrity
action_type: bounded_feature
risk_level: medium
repository: HarryWhite-TW/local-ai-workbench
branch: codex/workflow-final

records.title: evaluateFlag()'s depends_on recursion has no cycle detection — a circular flag dependency crashes the process
records.body:
**Where:** `src/lib/feature-flags.ts`, `evaluateFlag()`, "3. Check
dependencies" block:
```ts
if (flag.depends_on && flag.depends_on.length > 0) {
  for (const dep of flag.depends_on) {
    if (!evaluateFlag(dep, ctx).value) {   // recursive call, no visited-set / depth guard
      ...
    }
  }
}
```
**What's wrong:** `evaluateFlag` calls itself recursively to resolve each
dependency in `flag.depends_on`, with no cycle detection (no visited-flag
set, no recursion depth limit). `FlagDefinition.depends_on` is fully
attacker/admin-controllable via `POST /v1/admin/flags/load` and
`POST /v1/admin/flags/merge` (`middleware/featureFlags.ts`), which accept
and store an arbitrary `FlagSet` object with no validation of the
dependency graph. A flag set like:
```json
{ "a": { "enabled": true, "rollout_percentage": 100, "depends_on": ["b"] },
  "b": { "enabled": true, "rollout_percentage": 100, "depends_on": ["a"] } }
```
loaded via either endpoint, then evaluated once (e.g. via
`featureFlagContext`'s `isFeatureEnabled`, which runs on every request once
a route calls it, or directly via `GET /v1/admin/flags/:name`) causes
infinite mutual recursion — `evaluateFlag("a")` → `evaluateFlag("b")` →
`evaluateFlag("a")` → ... — until the call stack overflows and the process
crashes (`RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`, uncaught since
there's no guard).

**Impact:** a misconfigured (or malicious, given this is reachable through
an admin endpoint only protected by `ipWhitelist`+`adminLimiter` — no
`requestSigning`, per the separately-filed inconsistency issue) flag
payload can crash the entire backend process, not just fail the one
request.

**Suggested fix:** track visited flag names in a `Set` passed through the
recursive calls (or convert to an iterative topological check) and return
a `dependency_cycle` (or similar) `EvaluationResult` instead of recursing
further when a flag is revisited within the same evaluation.

records.title: Planner forwards all prior task outputs to every task, regardless of depends_on
records.body:
`_build_knowledge_aware_task` (`sources/core/planner.py:357`) prepends the `final_answers` of every completed task in `task_history` to each new task prompt (call site `:837`). `depends_on` is consulted only for scheduling (`_can_execute_step`, `:652`) and display; it never filters what a task gets to read. The effective information flow is therefore dense all-to-downstream while the plan declares a sparse graph.

Three consequences:

1. Topology legibility, the concern raised against compaction in #161, in the opposite direction: the workflow graph the judge and meta-orchestrator see is not the topology that ran. A task's outcome can depend on an answer from a task it does not declare.
2. Context growth by construction: a task late in an n-step plan carries all n-1 predecessors' answers whether relevant or not. This is the concentration #176 penalises, but the cause sits upstream of selection, since there is no handoff specification for the pressure to act on.
3. Evolvability: what a task forwards downstream is not part of the genotype, so it cannot be searched.

Recent empirical support that this is where gains live: Lee et al. (arXiv:2607.15524) co-evolve model and harness on ML research tasks; the converged harnesses replace full-history sharing with task-dependent communication contracts, and the authors attribute their gains primarily to inter-agent information-flow management rather than longer traces.

Proposal, in increasing order of ambition; the first two are small and default-inert:

1. Measure: log, per task, how many tokens each predecessor's answers contribute to the prompt (`_build_knowledge_aware_task` already holds the strings). This makes the effective graph visible next to the declared one.
2. Restrict, behind a flag: a config option (`knowledge_flow: all | dependencies`, defaulting to `all`) that limits the knowledge sections to `depends_on`, optionally transitive. The default keeps behaviour bit-identical.
3. Evolve: make the forwarded content per edge part of the plan schema, so selection, including the pressure in #176, can act on the handoff itself rather than only on its symptom.

Happy to send 1 and 2 as a PR if the direction looks right.

records.title: EPIC: Corpus Map → classify, deduplicate, place, sequence, review, and deliver knowledge
records.body:
# E.I.L — Corpus-First Execution Plan

## North Star
Build E.I.L as a corpus-first learning system. The current 18 uploaded files are **sources**, not chapters. They are the seed corpus from which the knowledge map and future learning sequence emerge. The number of future chapters is unbounded.

The primary product capability we are building now is:

> Given any new topic, image, article, note, document, or source, E.I.L can tell whether the idea already exists in the corpus, where it belongs in the knowledge map, what it overlaps with, what is genuinely new, and where it may eventually belong in the learning sequence.

## Product laws
- Sources are immutable evidence, not chapters.
- Concepts are canonical and deduplicated across sources.
- A single source can contribute to many concepts.
- A single concept can be supported by many sources.
- Taxonomy is discovered/refined from the corpus; it is not prematurely frozen.
- Topic classification and learning-sequence placement are separate decisions.
- The learning path is dependency-driven and spiral; it is not file-order-driven and not fixed to 18 chapters.
- Facts, evidence, models, interpretations, creator insights, beliefs/worldview claims, open questions, and tools must remain distinguishable.
- UI work is frozen until the corpus model and ingestion loop are stable.

## Phase 0 — Freeze and reset
- [ ] Do not merge the current product-spaces UI foundation as the new product truth.
- [ ] Mark the recent Home/Library/Dashboard work as exploratory/prototype only.
- [ ] Keep reusable backend/source/provenance work.
- [ ] Establish this issue as the active execution source of truth.

### Acceptance
There is one unambiguous active architecture direction: corpus → map → relations → sequence → learning experience.

---

## Phase 1 — Inventory the 18-source seed corpus
- [ ] Locate the canonical originals for all 18 uploaded source files.
- [ ] Assign each source a stable source ID and provenance metadata.
- [ ] Verify exact/lossless source retention where possible.
- [ ] Record title, type, author/origin if known, hash, ingestion date, language, and parsing status.
- [ ] Produce a corpus inventory report with missing/duplicate/problematic files called out explicitly.

### Acceptance
Every one of the 18 files is accounted for as a source; no file is treated as a chapter merely because of its file number.

---

## Phase 2 — Atomic extraction
For each source, extract reviewable atomic units instead of one summary.

- [ ] Claims / propositions
- [ ] Concepts / entities
- [ ] Definitions
- [ ] Questions
- [ ] Models / frameworks
- [ ] Examples / stories
- [ ] Practices / tools
- [ ] Creator conclusions / personal insights
- [ ] Beliefs / worldview claims
- [ ] Research references / evidence references
- [ ] Contradictions / tensions / uncertainty

Each extracted unit must link back to its exact source fragment.

### Acceptance
We can open any extracted idea and trace it back to the exact original source fragment(s).

---

## Phase 3 — Canonical concept registry + duplicate/overlap engine
Create a canonical concept layer above raw extracted terms.

- [ ] Normalize synonyms and aliases without deleting original wording.
- [ ] Detect exact duplicates.
- [ ] Detect semantic near-duplicates.
- [ ] Detect partial overlap / extension.
- [ ] Detect contradiction.
- [ ] Detect genuinely new concepts.
- [ ] Score each match with confidence and evidence.
- [ ] Never auto-merge ambiguous concepts; send them to review.

Required verdicts for new input:
- `EXISTS` — substantially already represented
- `EXTENDS` — exists but adds meaningful depth/evidence
- `RELATED` — adjacent, not duplicate
- `CONFLICTS` — meaningfully contradicts existing material
- `NEW` — not represented sufficiently in the corpus
- `UNCERTAIN` — human/creator review required

### Acceptance
Given a concept/article fragment, the system can return a ranked list of existing concepts and a justified verdict.

---

## Phase 4 — Emergent knowledge map (Corpus Map v0.1)
Build the map from evidence rather than freezing a predetermined number of stages.

Initial **anchors to test against the corpus**, not immutable top-level categories:
- Why this inquiry/project began
- The individual human / internal system
- The human in relation to the external world
- Interdependence / systems / symbiosis
- Deeper conclusions, interpretations, worldview, and meaning
- Personal development, beliefs, identity, choices, goals, environment, and change
- General knowledge that expands or challenges thought

For every canonical concept:
- [ ] Topic cluster(s)
- [ ] Subtopic(s)
- [ ] Knowledge type
- [ ] Supporting/contradicting sources
- [ ] Related concepts
- [ ] Prerequisite concepts
- [ ] Possible downstream concepts
- [ ] Confidence of placement
- [ ] Review state

### Acceptance
The first Corpus Map is generated from the 18-source corpus and can change as new sources arrive.

---

## Phase 5 — Relation graph
Move from folders to relationships.

Minimum relationship types:
- `IS_A`
- `PART_OF`
- `DEPENDS_ON`
- `INFLUENCES`
- `REGULATES`
- `CAUSES_OR_CONTRIBUTES_TO`
- `CONTRADICTS`
- `SUPPORTS`
- `EXPLAINS`
- `EXAMPLE_OF`
- `APPLIES_TO`
- `REFRAMES`
- `PREREQUISITE_FOR`
- `REVISITED_BY`

Important example of the intended graph style:
`nervous system ↔ perception ↔ emotion ↔ belief ↔ behavior ↔ environment`

### Acceptance
A concept is understandable not only by its folder but by the network around it.

---

## Phase 6 — Learning dependency graph and spiral sequence
Only after the corpus map exists:

- [ ] Infer prerequisite knowledge.
- [ ] Identify concepts that can be introduced early in simple form.
- [ ] Identify concepts that should be revisited later in deeper context.
- [ ] Separate `topic location` from `learning appearance` — one concept may appear many times in the journey.
- [ ] Build candidate learning units dynamically from clusters and dependencies.
- [ ] Do not impose a fixed chapter count.

A lear

records.title: Reimplement Parser with recursive-descent library
records.body:
The handwritten parser is good but any extensions on it are perhaps starting to get a bit difficult to understand; lots of conditionals and magic strings.

The parser could be made more legible (albeit more slow) by reimplementing with [Sprache](https://github.com/sprache/Sprache). A good alternative is N. Blumhardt's other parser [Superpower](https://github.com/datalust/superpower), but note that I do already have a [Markdown parser implemented in Sprache](https://github.com/IanWold/SpracheDown) that would be a good starting point.

Two options open for discussion there: either the markdown parser could be modified to return CFWeaver AST models, and the erroneous parts of the parser removed. Alternately, a transformer could be written to build the CFWeaver AST _from_ the generated Markdown AST, which would be more complicated but would have the advantage of being MD-parser-agnostic.

Leaning towards the former option (include custom parser) for the sake of being able to have more control over the parsing.

records.title: [P2][Frontend] Split the release bundle and enforce a chunk-size budget
records.body:
## Problem

The frontend release build succeeds but Vite reports that the main JavaScript chunk exceeds its 500 kB advisory threshold.

## Evidence

On the dependency-ordered frontend quality-gate slice (parent PR #48 head `94772ad03f5c37a00c1e3efa8a813229a7bf9845`), the pinned Node 22.22.2 build reports:

```text
dist/assets/index-*.js  621.62 kB | gzip: 190.81 kB
(!) Some chunks are larger than 500 kB after minification.
```

The application currently imports all routes eagerly, and the mapping workflow includes Monaco Editor in the main dependency graph.

## Required work

- Measure the production bundle by chunk and identify the largest contributors.
- Lazy-load route pages and load Monaco only when the mapping workflow needs it.
- Define an explicit, evidence-backed chunk budget and make CI fail on regression rather than suppressing Vite's warning.
- Preserve authenticated navigation, mapping behavior, and existing browser-console cleanliness.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The release build emits no unexplained oversized-chunk warning.
- [ ] Initial-route JavaScript is materially smaller, with before/after raw and gzip evidence.
- [ ] A deterministic CI budget detects future regressions.
- [ ] Unit tests and critical browser smoke remain green.
- [ ] No threshold is raised merely to silence the warning.

## Sequencing

Land after the frontend build/lint/test gate tracked by #23. This performance slice should not block that P0 correctness gate.
